articles.headline: Britain and Japan Discover Inflation Is Also Available in Their Currencies
articles.dek: UK inflation hit 3.5% and Japan's core rate reached 2.1%, and both central banks now appear ready to raise rates, though for different reasons and with different tax plans.
articles.catch_up: Energy prices have surged since the U.S.-Iran war disrupted oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. That shock is now showing up in consumer price data in Britain and Japan, two countries that import much of their energy.
articles.why_it_matters: If the Bank of England raises rates to 4% as markets expect, mortgages and business loans in Britain are likely to get more expensive. In Japan, higher inflation and a weak yen mean that imported fuel and goods cost more, even as the government cuts taxes.
body: UK consumer prices rose 3.5% in the 12 months to September, the Office for National Statistics said on Wednesday, above the 3.4% economists polled by Reuters had expected. CNBC reported that the figure follows 3.1% in August and 2.9% in July, and is the highest annual reading in almost a year. Motor fuel prices rose 29.8% over the year, a pace not seen since August 2022, so drivers are once again learning that a pump is a very effective way to read macroeconomic data.

Britain is a net energy importer. Translation: it buys more energy than it sells, so when the world price jumps, it pays the difference personally. The cause cited is the U.S.-Iran war and the struggle to move oil through the Strait of Hormuz, which is a long way from a Tesco forecourt but not from its price board.

The Bank of England is not expected to stop at the headline number. Scott Gardner of J.P. Morgan Personal Investing said services inflation has accelerated, which raises concern about "second round inflationary effects beyond energy prices." Translation: the worry is that higher fuel costs leak into wages, rents and everything else, and prices begin rising simply because everyone expects them to. Markets price a 98% chance of a 25 basis point hike to 4% next month, according to LSEG data. Translation: a basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point, so this is a quarter-point increase, and traders consider it nearly settled.

Chancellor John Healey has to present his first Autumn Budget next week, and the numbers are not helping. Separate data showed national debt exceeded £3 trillion for the first time in September, while the cost of servicing it has risen sharply and growth is weak. Healey promised to maintain "fiscal discipline" while giving families and businesses "breathing space." Those two goals are in tension, which is why Suren Thiru of the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales called the Budget "a perilous high-wire act." Higher inflation adds pressure for cost-of-living support and also pushes up borrowing costs, shrinking what Treasury officials call headroom, which is the gap between the government's plans and its self-imposed limits.

Japan's version is milder in size but similar in discomfort. Core inflation, which excludes fresh food, reached 2.1% in September, up from 1.7% in August, its highest this year. The Bank of Japan's preferred gauge, which also strips out energy, came in at 2.4%, above the central bank's 2% target. Capital Economics' Abhijit Surya noted that this happened even as rice prices fell 20.6% and energy prices fell 0.6%, thanks to subsidies from the Takaichi administration.

The pressure comes from imports. A weak yen makes oil and other goods more expensive, and Japan is buying energy from costlier U.S. sources as it moves away from Middle Eastern suppliers. Surya sees another rate hike in December after September's quarter-point increase to 1.25%, a three-decade high. For a country that spent decades trying to produce inflation, getting it must feel like receiving a long-awaited package with the wrong contents.

Meanwhile, Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama told parliament that Japan was "on the cusp of shifting to a period of sustained inflation driven by rising wages." Asked whether a plan to cut the consumption tax on food from 8% to 1% for two years clashes with rate hikes, he said he saw "no gap" between the government and the central bank, Reuters reported. One side is making food cheaper while the other makes borrowing dearer to cool prices, and they have apparently agreed this is coordination.
Watch the Budget next week, then the Bank of England's November meeting. Both governments want to cushion consumers from higher prices, and both central banks are preparing to do the opposite.
articles.wire_headline: UK inflation jumps to 3.5% — cementing rate hike expectations

articles.headline: Moderna Cancer Vaccine Works; Moderna Stock Falls 25% Anyway, Having Already Celebrated
articles.dek: Leaked partial data sent shares down as much as 25% even though full results showed a 42% cut in recurrence or death risk in melanoma patients.
articles.catch_up: Moderna and Merck are developing a personalized cancer vaccine, intismeran autogene, designed to be paired with Merck's immunotherapy Keytruda. Partial phase 3 data leaked on Thursday before the companies released the full results.
articles.why_it_matters: The episode shows how a stock priced for perfection can fall on good news, while patients and doctors judge the same data by a different standard. Investors in richly valued biotech names should note how little room expectations leave for anything short of a miracle.
body: Moderna shares fell as much as 25% on Thursday after partial data from its melanoma vaccine trial leaked, CNBC reported. The full data, released later that day, showed the shot paired with Keytruda cut the risk of recurrence or death by 42% compared with Keytruda alone. The market, having reviewed a result that doctors called a huge development, sold the stock.

Some numbers for those who prefer them to adjectives. About 82% of patients on the combination were alive without their melanoma returning at two years, versus 70% on Keytruda alone, according to the companies. The risk of the cancer spreading to distant parts of the body or death fell 38%. After the full six-month vaccine regimen, a separate analysis showed a 58% reduction in risk of recurrence or death.

Dr. Hussein Tawbi, a trial investigator at MD Anderson, called the results "a huge development for our patients," and noted the added benefit came with much milder side effects, such as injection-site pain. Translation: the treatment worked, it was tolerable, and the people most qualified to judge it were pleased. The people qualified to price it were not.

The explanation, offered by several analysts, is expectations. BMO Capital Markets analyst Evan Seigerman wrote that the reaction likely reflected "inflated expectations into the full data release," not a true indictment of the therapy. UBS likewise called it a strong data set and blamed the drop on massive expectations. Translation: a sell-the-news reaction, in which investors buy a stock for months in anticipation of good news and sell it the moment the news arrives, because nobody is left to buy.

The expectations had a visible address. Moderna shares had risen more than 530% this year as of Thursday afternoon, so even after a drop of up to 25%, the stock was presumably still living well. Merck, a much larger company, fell about 1% and is up nearly 41% this year. Size, it turns out, is a sedative.

There is also genuine caution in the science, and the executives said so. The companies say it is too early to know whether the treatment helps patients live longer overall. Merck research chief Dr. Dean Li said one result was like knocking down one tree, which "does not give you a cabin or a village." The vaccine is being tested in lung, bladder and kidney cancers, and UBS said these data increase confidence in the kidney and bladder studies.

Manufacturing is the other practical hurdle. Because each shot is built around the mutations in an individual patient's tumor, production can take six weeks. Merck CEO Robert Davis told CNBC the company believes it can shorten that timeline. Patients with melanoma are not in a position to be impressed by a leak; they would like the six weeks to be fewer.

The detailed results are due at the European Society for Medical Oncology conference this weekend. Watch whether the full presentation changes any minds on Monday, or whether the market simply finds a new figure to be disappointed by.
articles.wire_headline: Moderna shares plunge after cancer vaccine data leaks — despite positive results
